newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - British film makers bet on lottery boost.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - British film makers bet on lottery boost.

text.p: Britain's embattled film industry, overrun by Hollywood imports, has rallied its forces in recent years with hits like "Four Weddings and a Funeral" and "The English Patient".
But the flag-waving that has greeted those global hits has masked a less flattering truth. In terms of financial ownership, neither film is fully British.
Despite its British cast and director, "The English Patient" got its financial lifeblood from Miramax, part of U.S. giant Walt Disney Co's empire.
And "Four Weddings" -- which broke British box office records when it was first shown here -- got most of its financing from a unit of PolyGram NV, a majority-owned Dutch company.
"The money from 'Four Weddings and a Funeral' -- where is it? Show me where that is," Wilf Stevenson, director of the British Film Institute, told Reuters.
"'The English Patient' is the same. The money's gone back to Disney. That's great for Disney. They may reinvest in the UK in the future. But there's no guarantee of that," he added.
BRITISH FILM INDUSTRY LACKS LOCAL INVESTMENT
With few exceptions, Britain lacks local investment vehicles to transform its boom-and-bust cottage film industry into a consistent force in world cinema.
But that may start to change on May 15, when the Arts Council of England will award nearly 160 million pounds ($260 million) of national lottery funds to four film consortia.
This unprecedented sum, spread out over six years, marks a sharp increase from the estimated 30 million pounds of lottery funding invested in films over the past two years.
Under the plan, winning groups will each receive up to 39 million pounds of lottery funds over a six-year-period.

The franchises have attracted 37 bids, including one from a group formed by heavy hitters such as Merchant Ivory Production, Capitol Films, merchant bank Guinness Mahon, EMI Music Publishing and pop singer Elton John's Rocket Pictures.

Although bidding is not restricted to local firms, many industry insiders expect the funding to go to British groups that can produce and distribute a slate of films, thus enabling them to offset losses from flops with profits from hits.
"Over years -- and it will be a question of years -- you might see the emergence of mini-studios," said Charles Denton, chairman of the Arts Council's film panel.

"Not on the kind of scale that you have in the U.S., but on a scale which would provide a base for British film-makers and new talent rather than constantly having to start at the bottom of the hill with every individual film," he added.
FILM MAKERS STRUGGLE TO FIND DISTRIBUTORS
Currently, most British movie makers have to scrape together financing on a film-by-film basis, hoping that once made, their films can find a distributor to put them on the silver screen.

"The film industry is often characterised as being a film production industry. It isn't. It's a distribution industry. The costs are in production. But the money's in distribution," said the BFI's Stevenson.
And despite its recent revival, Britain's film industry suffers from an image problem among London's financiers.
"The City sees it as a very small industry," said Premila Hoon, director of media and entertainment finance at Guinness Mahon, which is very active in financing films.
"The film industry is fragmented, it's not vertically integrated, it's not efficient, and it's hard to estimate what your returns are going to be," she added.
One notable exception is Channel Four Films, part of the television company Channel Four, which has a British distribution unit among its operations.
This unit lets Channel Four reap more profits from the films it finances, such as last year's hit, "Trainspotting", and its one-third stake in "Four Weddings".

"The most important thing is that I'm also fully financing more films, and that way the money is coming back to the channel when they're succesful rather than going abroad," said David Aukin, head of film at Channel Four.
But the odds are high against other British film makers.
According to industry estimates, nearly half of British films fail to reach cinemas within a year of completion.
And less than one-third (31 percent) of British movies are put on wide release, meaning that they are shown on 30 or more screens across the country.
LOTTERY FUNDS SOWN AS "SEED MONEY"
The lottery financing should help matters by providing British film makers with systematic "seed money" that will attract other investors to projects.
The film industry has generally praised the plan, but some critics have called it a subsidy that is unlikely to produce more marketable movies.
"The idea of throwing money at individual productions is flying in the face of all learned experience from all over the world. I think it's just crazy," said Stevenson.
The Arts Council counters by arguing that the lottery funds are an investment rather than a grant or subsidy.
"The Arts Council has an expectation -- however that may be met, only time will tell -- of recoupment and indeed sharing in net profits," Denton said.
And as long as the films earn returns for investors, British movie makers should be able to find financing, whether from local or overseas sources.

"At the end of the day, If the British observe that the French and the Germans and the Americans are doing rather well out of British movies, then maybe they'll think it's time for them to move in as well," said Channel Four's Aukin.
"But it doesn't really worry me," he added. "Money has no flag attached to it."
